chicken-thigh-rotisserie-skin-not-eaten.title: Chicken thigh, rotisserie, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken thigh prepared by rotisserie (spit‑roasting) with the skin removed. The meat is flavorful, tender and juicy thanks to the slow, even rotation over an open flame. This cooking method preserves most nutrients while giving the meat a distinctive smoky taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rotisserie cooking uses a vertical spit that ensures uniform heat from all sides.
Chicken thighs contain more iron and zinc than chicken breast.
Removing the skin reduces saturated fat and overall calorie content.
Rotisserie meat is a staple of street food cultures worldwide, from the US to Turkey and Japan.
Proper marination can keep rotisserie thighs up to 30 % juicier than baked pieces.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken thigh provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: It supplies vitamin B6 and niacin, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: The meat is a good source of iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood health and bones.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Skin‑less thighs contain less saturated fat, making them suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Selenium present in chicken helps maintain a healthy immune response.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improper cooking may leave pathogens such as Salmonella. Cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the thighs are marinated, sodium levels can be high, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Histamine formation
items.content: Extended storage can lead to histamine buildup, causing food intolerance.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skin‑less rotisserie chicken thigh can be served hot as a main dish, sliced into salads, sandwiches, tacos, or added to stews. It stores well sliced thin and kept refrigerated for up to three days.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked meat in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C for no more than 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a zip‑lock bag at –18 °C for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 74 °C before consuming.

content.title: About
content.content: Coconut milk is made by grinding the flesh of ripe coconuts and squeezing out the liquid. It is a thick, mildly sweet beverage widely used in Asian cooking. It serves as a dairy alternative, giving dishes a creamy texture and a distinctive coconut aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Coconut milk is different from coconut water, which is the clear liquid inside the fruit.
Traditionally it was prepared by hand using a grater and cheesecloth.
In South‑Asian cuisine it appears in curries, soups, desserts, and drinks.
There are two main types: thin (diluted with water) and thick (concentrated).
Coconut milk can be fermented to make coconut yogurt.

items.title: Rich in medium‑chain triglycerides
items.content: These fats are quickly metabolized and can support energy levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B3 and B6 help normal metabolism.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Coconut milk provides iron, magnesium, potassium and zinc, important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Lactose‑free
items.content: Suitable for people with lactose intolerance and vegans.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phenolic compounds help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Although the fats are beneficial, excess intake can contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Coconut allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions, including skin rashes and swelling.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Coconut milk is calorie‑rich, so portion control is advised, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Sodium in canned versions
items.content: Ready‑to‑use canned milk often contains added salt, which is undesirable for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add coconut milk to curries, soups, sauces, smoothies and desserts. It can replace cream in baking or serve as a base for vegan ice cream. Before use, shake or stir to restore a uniform consistency.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store an opened carton in the refrigerator for up to 4‑5 days. Canned coconut milk, once opened, can be transferred to an airtight container and kept for up to 7 days. Freeze in portion‑size bags for longer storage.

content.title: About
content.content: Hominy are whole corn kernels that have been treated with an alkaline solution (usually calcium hydroxide) to remove the hull and germ. After the nixtamalization process the kernels are boiled until tender. Hominy has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a pleasantly chewy texture. It is used in soups, stews, salads, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hominy is a staple in Mexican cuisine, most famously in pozole, and in Southern U.S. cooking for dishes like hominy grits.
Alkaline processing increases the bioavailability of minerals such as iron and zinc.
Hominy can be yellow or white depending on the corn variety.
Unlike corn flakes, hominy retains most of its dietary fiber.
In the United States hominy is often sold canned and ready to eat.

items.title: Rich in complex carbohydrates
items.content: Hominy provides slowly digestible carbs that help maintain steady blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Provides magnesium
items.content: Magnesium aids normal muscle and nerve function and participates in energy production.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Hominy is virtually fat‑free, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products, including hominy.

items.title: Sodium content in canned versions
items.content: Canned hominy often contains added salt; people watching sodium intake should choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Alkaline processing
items.content: Those sensitive to alkaline‑treated foods may experience digestive discomfort.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add hominy to soups, chili, salads, serve it as a side with meat or fish, or bake it into casseroles. Dried kernels are typically boiled for 20‑30 minutes until tender before use.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry hominy in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Once opened, canned hominy should be kept in the refrigerator in a sealed container and used within 3‑4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Baked plain potato chips are thin slices of potato dried in an oven at low temperature. They have a crunchy texture, a subtle natural potato flavor, and contain far less fat than their fried counterparts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Baking reduces the fat content by up to 70 % compared with traditional deep‑frying.
These chips are often used as a base for diet‑friendly snacks and culinary experiments.
In the United States baked chips gained popularity in the early 2000s as a healthier alternative.
There are many variants: seasoned, herb‑infused, and plain – as in this product.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Baking limits the amount of added oil, making the chips less calorie‑dense.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports fluid balance and heart function.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Although some vitamin C is lost during heating, small amounts remain.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑potato chips retain some fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: No artificial additives
items.content: This product contains no artificial flavors or preservatives.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience an allergic reaction to potato.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Unsalted versions are safe, but salted varieties should be consumed within daily sodium limits.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes have a high glycemic index, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the chips as a standalone snack, add them to salads, use them in recipes as a breadcrumb substitute, or as a crunchy base for dips.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, store in the refrigerator to maintain crispness and prevent moisture absorption.

content.title: About
content.content: Tomato soup is a hot dish made from ripe tomatoes, broth, vegetables, and spices. It has a bright aroma, rich flavor, and characteristic red color. The soup can be served as a standalone meal or as part of a menu in restaurants and cafeterias.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato soup became popular in Europe in the 19th century when tomatoes became widely available.
In Italy, a classic tomato‑based soup is "minestrone" with beans and pasta added.
Tomatoes for soup are often roasted before simmering to deepen the flavor.
Tomato soup is frequently topped with croutons, grated Parmesan, or fresh herbs.
A cold version called gazpacho is a staple in Spain.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health and may reduce the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: Vitamins A and C
items.content: Tomato soup provides vitamin A for vision and vitamin C for immune function.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: A serving of soup is low in calories, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from tomatoes and vegetables aids normal digestive processes.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The high water content helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes, ranging from skin rashes to swelling.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Tomatoes are acidic and can aggravate heartburn or reflux in sensitive people.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared soup often contains added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve tomato soup hot, often accompanied by croutons, sour cream, grated cheese, or fresh herbs. It can be made ahead and reheated, or used as a base for more complex dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the soup to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 2 months. Reheat to a rolling boil before serving.
